libghostty-vt 1.0 is here. libghostty is a
portable, high-performance C library for terminal emulation, extracted
directly from the core of Ghostty. The 1.0 release means both the library
itself and the C ABI are now stable.A little over a year ago, I wrote that
libghostty is coming. At the time,

but Ghostty was a consumer. Today, the C API is a complete terminal emulator,
it runs in production for millions of people across hundreds of products,
both free and commercial, and it has a real, enforced ABI stability policy.This post is about how we got here and what 1.0 actually means.1Since starting the Ghostty project in 2022, the most common question I've

libghostty is coming
post, so feel free to read that if you wish. Today, I'd rather answer this

We escaped it and achieved code execution as root on the host.We found how it saved registers, changed where it would resume, and made it execute a call of our choosing when it returned from KVM. The guest then restored the temporary stack changes. Firecracker kept running, and the VM remained accessible over SSH.PwnEscape Part 1 introduced the host memory primitive behind this work. Here we follow the next part of the chain: using that access to find Firecracker in memory and take over a live thread from inside the guest. This is a continuation to show CVE-2026-99999 on a Firecracker setup.A Firecracker microVM has a process on the host that manages it. Each virtual CPU, or vCPU, has a thread in that process. The thread enters KVM to run the guest and returns to Firecracker when an event needs handling in userspace. title: AI is dramatically accelerating AI research (planned-obsolescence.org)
comments: As somebody who does ML research, LLMs certainly make ML research faster. Maybe even 10x in some cases, as the author suggests.But that’s just the parts of ML research that take place within your compute environment, namely experiments on model architecture, training strategy, UI/UX, etc. The algorithms and software.Just because that part of research is progressively accelerated does not imply that we’re on a collision course with world-ending “superintelligence”. It just means that you’ll get to the best possible model of your data faster. And even when your data is the entire corpus of textual knowledge, there is a limit to the utility that provides.It just means that software engineering, data analysis, and other computational tasks will be less of a bottleneck in the overall progress of the world (which, by the way, is great, and extremely valuable).I don’t think it’s a stretch to say that we’ll have reached max LLM capability within a couple of years (what the author refers to as “super intelligence”). But it is a huge logical leap to say this:> If we go through this feedback loop, I expect that the AI systems that come out the other side will be able to very quickly develop novel weapons and very easily overpower human civilization in a conflict.First of all, the weapons necessary to overpower human civilization exist. They aren’t used as such due to geopolitics and humans’ basic survival instinct. Second, developing novel weapons requires physical tests, which are decidedly not accelerated by LLMs.AI is a tool wielded by humans. If we’re wiped out by AI, it will be at the direction of a human. But we’ve made it pretty far with some pretty unstable humans in command of planet-killer weapons. I’m not overly concerned.reply

LLMs can't access materials for developing weapons without weapons tests conducted at their behest, and humans choose not to - of their own volition - use world-ending weapons.Let's also imagine for the purpose of conversation that one of the things that can be gotten at an extremely high skill level through increased intelligence is the power of persuasion.A "superintelligence" persuades humans to perform weapons tests and then to give it the ability to use the weapon.I think everything you've said is reasonable except the bit where you think step one of an "AI" exterminating humanity wouldn't look like a human doing it. In my opinion, the most likely vector for disaster is a human being who is "guided" by a computer model to do something unfortunate, not the model doing so directly.reply

VFAT is the way that some operating systems implement long filenames in FAT - PROGRA~1 and whatnot. It's pretty messy.reply

Not really, no.  Linux regards various ways of looking at the same on-disc filesystem format as distinct filesystem types: msdos, umsdos, vfat.  Old Microsoft doco from the 1990s that is still lying around explains things in the way that they historically progressed rather than structurally, describing VFAT as an extension of FAT32.The reality, certainly in respect of the headlined subject, is that the bitness of the FAT and the style of the root directory (fixed location or variable length) are the only meaningful variants.  In 2026, no-one aims not to support long filenames on FAT, and EFI understands them natively.  EFI copes with all three bitnesses.  And it does the conventional thing of variable length root directory on 32-bit and fixed-length root directory on 16-bit and 12-bit.FAT is a very poor filesystem format, and no, it's not a minimum filesystem format if one is writing one's own operating system.  It's a lazy filesystem format, inasmuch as the cross-development tooling for it exists.  But if one were writing a minimum filesystem for one's own operating system, one could start from much better places.  FAT is not minimal by any reasonable definition even if one is not writing one's own operating system, and requires an awful lot of hoops to be jumped through that are only there because one is being compatible with the cross-development tooling, several decades of historical changes, and whatnot.One could use the original UFS, for example.  LEAN exists.  Over 20 years ago, I invented HPFS2.* https://jdebp.uk/Proposals/hpfs2.htmlreply

title: Panthera: Ampere's CPU Performance Model (github.com/amperecomputing)
comments: > Panthera represents low-background steel for computer systems. It is an end-to-end, industrial-grade performance model conceived, designed, and hand-crafted entirely by human architects before the era of generative AI. This repository represents over 8 years of work and 6000 individual git commits by 45 people. By making this human-authored codebase public, we hope it serves as a trusted, high-watermark reference for human engineers and future automated hardware-modeling tools alike.reply

This is a cycle accurate simulator. It takes a list of instructions and simulates how long it would take to actually execute those instructions. In addition it keeps track of counters for various things (cache misses, interrupts, etc). Correlation refers to making sure the counter values reported by the sim are within some ballpark of the same values on a real chip. Cycle accurate sims are used for  architecture research (trying out new features) as well as pre-silicon software work - chip isn't taped out but you want to start building a compiler. They are generally very slow (1000x slower than running on device) because they are generally written by HW people who have no idea how to write fast code. I would be interested to know how fast this one is.reply
